topics.title: Transpiling, bundling, and type checking — why can a broken TypeScript app still build?
topics.html:
A frontend toolchain performs several different jobs. Success at one stage does not establish correctness at the others.

  • Transpiling transforms source syntax into executable JavaScript and can remove TypeScript annotations without checking their meaning.
  • Bundling follows module dependencies and produces deployable resources, often with splitting and optimization.
  • Type checking analyzes whether the code follows the static contracts. Vite’s TypeScript transform is not a substitute for a separate type check.
  • Tests examine selected runtime behavior. A successful type check cannot prove that a server contract, interaction, or accessibility behavior works.

Give each required check a clear CI command and make a failed check block publication. Do not rely on the developer having noticed an editor warning. The snippet is a conventional Vite application pipeline, not a requirement to add Vite to a buildless static site.

{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit",
    "test": "vitest run",
    "build": "npm run typecheck && vite build"
  }
}
In plain words

A tool can remove a type annotation without proving that it was correct. I keep static checks, runtime tests, and the production build explicit, then require the appropriate checks before publishing.

Does transpiling syntax add every missing browser API?
No. Converting syntax and providing runtime APIs are different concerns. Check the target environments and add a deliberate compatibility strategy for APIs the application actually uses.
Can local editor errors be ignored because CI is green?
A green pipeline is meaningful only for the checks it runs and the files it includes. Compare the TypeScript configuration, generated inputs, runtime versions, and CI commands rather than assuming the editor or CI must be wrong.

  • TypeScript: compiler options

topics.title: Tree shaking — why did an unused import keep code, or remove required CSS?
topics.html:
Tree shaking uses the module graph and information about observable behavior to eliminate unused code. It is not equivalent to deleting every export that is not called directly in one file.

  • Static ES module imports and exports make analysis easier. Dynamic CommonJS patterns can make the result harder to determine.
  • An import can matter because evaluating the module registers something, modifies global state, or loads CSS.
  • The package’s sideEffects declaration tells the bundler which modules must retain their evaluation behavior. An incorrect “everything is pure” declaration can break production.
  • Tree shaking removes unused work; code splitting changes when retained code is loaded. A large actively used dependency may need splitting or replacement rather than a purity annotation.

Inspect the production output and test a consuming application. Development behavior can hide a packaging mistake. A barrel file is not automatically fatal, but re-export patterns and side effects can affect what a particular bundler can remove.

{
  "name": "example-ui-library",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": "./dist/index.js",
  "sideEffects": [
    "**/*.css",
    "./dist/register-elements.js"
  ]
}
In plain words

The bundler needs to know whether evaluating a module changes anything outside its exports. I preserve registration modules and styles deliberately, then verify the optimized consumer build instead of trusting a smaller byte count by itself.

Should I put sideEffects: false in every package?
Only when the claim is accurate for the published modules. Otherwise an optimizer may remove an import whose evaluation was required for correct behavior.
Will minifying an import-heavy page guarantee tree shaking?
No. Minification and module-level analysis are related optimizations, but they do not solve identical problems. Check the module format, package declarations, build mode, and actual output.

topics.title: Code splitting — where should you draw a lazy-loading boundary?
topics.html:
Split at a meaningful usage boundary, such as a route, a large editor, or a rarely opened report. The objective is less work before the current task becomes usable.

  • Dynamic import introduces an asynchronous module boundary that a bundler can turn into a separately loaded resource.
  • Declare React lazy components outside rendering so their identity is stable. A Suspense boundary supplies the loading experience.
  • Too many tiny chunks can create request overhead or waterfalls. Measure the network and execution impact rather than treating chunk count as a success metric.
  • Keep an error strategy for a failed chunk request. A Suspense fallback represents pending work; an Error Boundary handles a rejected load.

A deployed application may still have older HTML or an already running older client. Retain old hashed chunks long enough for that release strategy, or provide a bounded recovery path. Repeatedly reloading a broken release is not a reliable fix.

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const Reports = lazy(() => import('./Reports.js'));

export function ReportsRoute() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p role="status">Loading reports.</p>}>
      <Reports />
    </Suspense>
  );
}
// Reports.js provides a default component export.
// Place an appropriate Error Boundary above this route.
In plain words

I defer code the current task does not need, while keeping the loading and failure states deliberate. A good split makes the first task cheaper without making every later interaction wait through another chain of chunks.

Should the main above-the-fold screen always be lazy?
Not automatically. Deferring critical content can delay it. Measure which resources are essential for the first useful screen, and split code that is outside that path.
Why do chunk errors often appear immediately after deployment?
An older running client can request a hashed chunk that the new deployment removed. Check asset retention, HTML caching, base paths, and release consistency before treating it as an intermittent React bug.
Official references
  • React: lazy
  • Vite: production build and load errors

topics.title: Frontend environment variables — what is configuration and what is actually secret?
topics.html:
A value shipped to the browser is available to the person running that browser. A variable name, an env file, or minification does not change that boundary.

  • In Vite’s default setup, custom VITE_ values are exposed to client code. They are configuration, not a place for server credentials.
  • Custom env values arrive as strings: the string "false" is truthy. Parse and validate the values the application depends on.
  • Bundled configuration is typically substituted during the build. Changing a hosting environment variable does not rewrite an already published static JavaScript file.
  • If one artifact must work in several environments, design an explicit runtime-configuration resource and its validation and caching policy.

A private provider key belongs in a server-side integration that enforces the application’s access rules. Some services deliberately issue public client identifiers or restricted public keys; use the service’s documented model rather than assuming every value called “key” is interchangeable.

const apiBase = import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL;
if (typeof apiBase !== 'string' || apiBase.length === 0) {
  throw new Error('Missing API base URL');
}

const reportsEnabled = import.meta.env.VITE_REPORTS_ENABLED === 'true';

// Both values are public client configuration.
// Do not place a private service credential in a VITE_ variable.
In plain words

I treat frontend env values as public configuration that usually becomes part of the built artifact. If a value must remain private, it cannot be delivered to the browser in the first place.

Is a feature hidden by a client-side flag protected?
No. A flag can choose the UI experience, but the server must still authorize the operation. A person can inspect or modify client code and call the endpoint directly.
Why did changing an env value have no effect on the static site?
The existing bundle may contain the previous build-time value. Check the actual built artifact and deployment pipeline, then rebuild or use the runtime-configuration mechanism the application was designed to read.

  • Vite: production builds

topics.title: Lockfiles, version ranges, and peer dependencies — what makes installs reproducible?
topics.html:
A dependency range describes allowed versions. A lockfile records a resolved dependency graph. They answer different questions.

  • For a stable major version, ^1.2.3 permits compatible minor and patch updates below version 2; ~1.2.3 stays below 1.3. Pre-1.0 ranges have different compatibility boundaries.
  • Commit the package manager’s lockfile for an application. With npm, npm ci requires the manifest and lockfile to agree rather than silently repairing the lockfile.
  • Pin the intended runtime and package-manager versions in the workflow too. Native dependencies and platform-specific optional packages can still differ by environment.
  • A library’s peer dependency describes a compatible host dependency. This matters for React libraries, where shipping a separate incompatible React copy can break the runtime model.

Review dependency changes as code changes: why the package is needed, what runs during installation, what the update changes, and whether the published artifact contains the expected files. A clean vulnerability report is useful evidence, not proof that arbitrary code is trustworthy.

# A typical application's CI, with a committed package-lock.json:
npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build

# Dependency updates intentionally change the lockfile in a reviewed change.
# Do not replace npm ci with a lockfile-rewriting install just to hide a mismatch.
In plain words

The range says what is acceptable; the lockfile says what this installation resolved. I keep CI deterministic, update dependencies deliberately, and distinguish packages bundled by a library from packages the host application must provide.

Does npm ci guarantee identical output on every operating system?
No. It improves dependency resolution reproducibility, but platform conditions, native builds, tools, environment variables, and the runtime can still affect the result.
Why might two React copies cause an invalid Hook call?
Hooks depend on the renderer and the component using the expected React runtime instance. An incorrectly packaged dependency can bring another copy; inspect the dependency graph and peer dependency configuration.
Official references

  • npm: package.json dependency contracts
  • React: invalid Hook call
